title: The Change of Qiblah
subtitle: From Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ancient Kaaba and the Identity of the Median Community
summary: Sixteen months of facing Jerusalem in prayer, the Prophet's longing gaze toward the heavens, the revelation of Surah Al-Baqarah during midday prayer at Masjid al-Qiblatayn, the seamless rotation of the congregation, and the theological establishment of the Abrahamic spiritual center.

sections.text: For the first sixteen or seventeen months following the Hijrah to Madinah, the Muslim community directed their faces in every prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis—the sacred sanctuary of Jerusalem. The sirah says that in Makkah he had prayed on the southern side of the Kaaba so that Jerusalem also lay before him. That detail is sirah. In Madinah, however, which lay geographically situated directly between Makkah to the south and Jerusalem to the north, facing one sanctuary necessitated turning one's back directly upon the other.

The prayer toward Jerusalem kept the community on the qiblah associated with the earlier prophets. In Madinah that direction also became a point of argument. Reports in the sirah and in tafsir attribute to some of the Jews the saying, 'Muhammad differs with us in religion and follows our qiblah.' The Quran names the objectors only as the foolish among the people. Al-Bara's report in Bukhari 399 explains that phrase, in his wording, as the Jews. The boast is not treated here as one agreed verbatim record.
The ancient Kaaba in Makkah, the primordial sanctuary of Ibrahim, toward which the Prophet's heart yearned.

In his heart, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ yearned deeply to face the Kaaba in Makkah—the primordial House of God built by the patriarch of monotheism, Ibrahim, and his son Isma'il. It was the Qiblah of his father Ibrahim, free from all sectarian claims. Yet, being the epitome of spiritual discipline, he never presumed to alter the prayer direction on his own initiative or utter an impatient complaint; instead, he would frequently step outside into the night and gaze silently toward the celestial canopy, awaiting divine command.

Al-Bara, in Sahih al-Bukhari 399, says the Prophet prayed toward Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months, and that he loved to face the Kaaba, until God revealed, 'We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven,' and he turned toward the Kaaba. The sirah places the change around the middle of Sha'ban in the second year. That month is the historians' date, not a date stated in the hadith. The verse, in part, reads:

قَدْ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ فِي السَّمَاءِ ۖ فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبْلَةً تَرْضَاهَا ۚ فَوَلِّ وَجْهَكَ شَطْرَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ ۚ وَحَيْثُ مَا كُنتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ شَطْرَهُ
'We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven, and We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.' (part of Surah al-Baqarah 2:144; the verse continues)

These are separate reports, and they are not combined here into one timetable. In Bukhari 399 a man who had prayed with the Prophet went out and passed some of the Ansar praying Asr toward Jerusalem. He told them he had prayed with the Messenger facing the Kaaba, and they turned. The hadith does not say that the Prophet himself turned in the middle of a rak'ah, and it does not name that congregation as Quba.

In Bukhari 403, Abdullah ibn Umar says that the people at Quba were in the morning prayer when a man came and said that Quran had been sent down that night and that the Prophet had been commanded to face the Kaaba, so they should face it. Their faces were toward Syria, and they turned toward the Kaaba. This report does not say they were bowing, and it does not place the scene on the morning after a mid-prayer turn by the Prophet. Muslim 525, from al-Bara, says a man passed people of the Ansar who were praying and they turned toward the House. It does not name Quba. The telling that the Prophet turned one hundred and eighty degrees at Banu Salimah, and that Quba then turned the next morning while bowing, is how some sirah writers join the scenes. It is not stated as one sequence in these hadiths.
The serene architecture of early Madinan mosques where prayer united hearts across horizons.
The Median Community and Spiritual Independence

The Quran says the foolish among the people will ask what turned the Muslims from the qiblah they were on. In al-Bara's report in Bukhari 399 that phrase is explained, in his wording, as the Jews. The verse itself does not name one party. It is not accurate to give the objection only to the hypocrites.

سَيَقُولُ السُّفَهَاءُ مِنَ النَّاسِ مَا وَلَّاهُمْ عَن قِبْلَتِهِمُ الَّتِي كَانُوا عَلَيْهَا ۚ قُل لِّلَّهِ الْمَشْرِقُ وَالْمَغْرِبُ ۚ يَهْدِي مَن يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ
'The foolish among the people will say, "What has turned them away from the qiblah they were on?" Say: To God belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path.' (Surah al-Baqarah 2:142)

The next verse begins, and this is not the whole of it:
وَكَذَٰلِكَ جَعَلْنَاكُمْ أُمَّةً وَسَطًا لِّتَكُونُوا شُهَدَاءَ عَلَى النَّاسِ وَيَكُونَ الرَّسُولُ عَلَيْكُمْ شَهِيدًا
'And thus We have made you a middle community that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you…' (the opening of 2:143)

Facing the Kaaba set the prayer toward the House linked with Ibrahim. The community was no longer aligned on Jerusalem. What that meant for its relation to the earlier communities is a matter the Quran addresses in the verses around the change, including the witness of a middle community in the opening of 2:143, not in a single label.

references.title: The Holy Quran
references.author: Surah Al-Baqarah (2:142–144)
references.notes: Primary divine scriptural decree commanding the shift of the prayer direction toward Al-Masjid al-Haram.

references.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
references.author: Imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari (d. 256 AH)
references.source: Kitab al-Salat, Bab al-Tawajjuh Nahwa al-Qiblah Haythukana, Hadith 399 & Hadith 403
references.notes: Bukhari 399: sixteen or seventeen months toward Jerusalem, then the Kaaba; a man finds the Ansar at Asr and they turn. Bukhari 403: the people at Quba in the morning prayer turn when told the command came that night. The two reports are not one timetable.

references.title: Sahih Muslim
references.author: Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 261 AH)
references.source: Kitab al-Masajid wa Mawadi' al-Salat, Bab Tahwil al-Qiblah min Bayt al-Maqdis ila al-Ka'bah, Hadith 525
references.notes: Muslim 525: after the Prophet had prayed, a man passed Ansar who were praying and they turned toward the House. The hadith does not name Quba or a bow.
